text:
**Marginalia**

The first correction appeared in October, in a copy of *The Old Man and the Sea* that had circulated through the Kestrel Harbor library for eleven years without incident. Nadia found it while checking the book back in: a small, careful pencil mark in the margin beside a line about the Gulf Stream. *Currents shift north of the Keys,* the note read, in a hand so precise it looked typeset. *Santiago would have known this.*

She almost missed it. The pencil was soft, the pressure light, the handwriting small enough to hide under a thumb. But once she'd seen it, she started seeing them everywhere. A biography of lighthouse keepers came back with a date corrected—the author had written 1893 where the town records said 1891. A field guide to shorebirds had a note beside the drawing of a sanderling: *Legs are blacker in winter. The plate flatters them.* A novel set in a fishing village had a single word circled, with the comment *We say "gunkhole," not "creek,"* and Nadia, who had lived in Kestrel Harbor for six years, had to admit she'd never once heard anyone say "creek."

She should have been annoyed. Pencil in library books was vandalism, technically, even if it could be erased. But the corrections were never cruel, and they were always right. She checked the lighthouse date against the historical society's website. She checked the sanderling. She even asked a fisherman at the co-op about "gunkhole," and he laughed and said, "Where'd you hear that? My grandmother used to say it."

The books came back through the night drop, always on Tuesdays, always three or four at a time. Nadia started pulling the borrowing records, but the books were old, well-thumbed, popular in the way that books about the sea are popular in a town that lives on it. Dozens of names in the history. She narrowed it down by subject—local history, maritime, birds—and by who requested books through interlibrary loan when the library's own copies were out. The list shrank to a handful.

She didn't pursue it. That was the strange part. She told herself she was letting the mystery ripen, but the truth was she'd started to look forward to Tuesdays. She'd come in early, before the doors opened, and open the drop box like a kid opening a mailbox. Some weeks there were no notes, and she felt the absence like a skipped appointment.

Then, in January, a correction came back that wasn't a correction at all. It was in a book of poems by a man who had drowned off the point in 1974, a local writer the library kept in a special case because the high school checked it out every year. The note was beside a poem about the harbor in winter:

*My wife set this poem to music once. She never finished it. I think the third stanza resisted her.*

Nadia sat with the book for a long time, the radiator ticking, the windows gray with salt haze. She looked at the borrowing record. The book had been checked out to E. Voss.

There was one Voss in the phone book, or rather one V-E. Walter Voss, on Tern Street, which was the street where the houses got small and the water got close. She knew the name. Everyone of a certain age knew the name—Voss had taught English at the regional school for thirty years, and half the town had suffered through his comma drills. He'd retired before Nadia moved to town, and she'd seen him only in fragments: at the pharmacy, at the fish market, always alone, always with a canvas bag of books.

She didn't erase the notes. She started answering them.

The next Tuesday she left a pencil in the drop box—good one, a Mars Lumograph, with a note taped to it: *For the margins. The library thanks you for your service. —N.*

The following Tuesday, the pencil came back with a note of its own: *A librarian who abets vandalism. What is the world coming to. —W.V.*

After that, the books carried conversations. Nadia would leave a question in a margin—*Did you know the poet?*—and a week later, in different pencil, softer, she'd find the answer: *Everyone knew him. He came into the school and read to my seventh graders once. They were merciless. He was delighted.*

She learned things in fragments. That his wife's name was Ruth and she had died four years ago. That he had stopped teaching not because he wanted to but because his eyes had begun to fail, and that the pencil notes were large to him now, even if they looked small to Nadia. That he read with a magnifying sheet and enormous patience, one line at a time, the way you'd walk a beach after a storm.

In March, she broke the rules of the game. She wrote in the margin of the lighthouse book: *Come to the library. I'll make tea. I want to argue with you about the sanderling.*

A week passed. Then two. The drop box went quiet, and Nadia convinced herself she'd ruined it—that she'd turned a correspondence into a demand, and demands were the thing a man who lived alone on Tern Street had learned to live without.

Then, on a Tuesday, he came in. Not through the drop box but through the front door, at ten in the morning, when the library was empty except for the gulls walking the flat roof. He was smaller than she'd expected, in a wool coat that had outlived its shape, holding the canvas bag in both hands like a man reporting to a dock.

"You wrote in pencil," he said, by way of greeting. "In a library book. That's against the rules."

"So is correcting them," Nadia said.

"Correcting them is a public service." He set the bag on the counter. "I taught for thirty years. I can't stop. It's like breathing in a room full of sleeping students."

She made tea in the back room, in the electric kettle she kept for the book club, and they sat at the table by the microfiche machine nobody had used since the renovation. He was easier to talk to than she'd expected, and harder, in the way of people who listen carefully. He corrected her twice—once about the year the pier was rebuilt, once about the name of a gull—and both times he was right, and both times she wrote it down.

"Why the night drop?" she asked. "You could have come in all along."

He looked at his hands. "Ruth and I came here every Saturday for forty years. She'd take the novels, I'd take the history. She'd read me the good sentences out loud in the car." He turned his cup
